clue.text: Thomson's view of liberty?

parts.note: James Thomson's long poem Liberty has a part titled The ..., and a view across country is a word for exactly that sight

explanation.walkthrough: James Thomson (author of The Seasons) wrote the poem Liberty, whose last part is The Prospect; a prospect is also simply a view.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide outlook over landscape is called a prospect, and Thomson named a section of his poem Liberty with that word.

clue.text: Miss Pargeter entered his field

parts.note: Edith Pargeter, writing as Ellis Peters, titled a Brother Cadfael mystery after a craftsman's burial ground for strangers

explanation.walkthrough: Edith Pargeter (Ellis Peters) wrote The Potter's Field, a Cadfael novel; 'entered his field' reads as joining a craftsman's trade but means she wrote about the biblical burial plot.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical burial ground bought with Judas's silver is named for a clay-working craftsman, and Pargeter's novel takes that title.

clue.text: Order duck first for instrumentalist

annotationWithheld.why: Order duck first for instrumentalist: duck gives O and first gives IST, but no reading of 'Order' supplies the remaining BO, so the clue as held looks misread

clue.text: Youngest son of the "mobled queen"

parts.note: the mobled queen is Hecuba in the Player's speech in Hamlet; her youngest boy was murdered by Polymestor of Thrace

explanation.walkthrough: 'The mobled queen' is Hamlet's phrase for Hecuba, queen of Troy; her youngest son was sent away for safety and killed by the Thracian king.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Priam and Hecuba's last-born boy carries this name, and Euripides' Hecuba opens with his ghost.

clue.text: A topical Bond adapted by Sabatini

indicators.note: a work adapted is changed into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A film-maker has turned a timely James Bond story into something new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' looks like 007, but A TOPICAL BOND is the fodder; 'adapted' rearranges its twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rafael Sabatini wrote the 1922 pirate novel of this title, later filmed with Errol Flynn.

clue.text: US writer accompanying president

parts.note: the novelist's first name was Truman, so his surname follows the name of President Truman

explanation.walkthrough: The writer is Truman Capote: his surname literally accompanies the name of the thirty-third president.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of In Cold Blood bore the first name Truman, so his family name stands next to that president's name.

clue.text: Psychiatrist caught in some cradle robbery

indicators.note: caught in some says a run of letters is trapped inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A psychiatrist has been arrested for snatching babies.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Psychiatrist caught' as the definition, but 'caught' belongs with 'in some' as the hiding signal; the run is cr(ADLE R)obbery.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Adler, a Viennese founder of individual psychology, was an early colleague of Freud.

clue.text: Mother of Cleopatra and Alexander to be seen in London arena on Saturday

parts.note: Olympia is an exhibition hall and arena in west London
S is the standard abbreviation for Saturday

explanation.surface: Royal relatives of ancient Macedon might turn up at a London venue at the weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: Olympia is a large exhibition centre in Kensington, London. This Cleopatra is Alexander the Great's sister, not the Egyptian queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip II's wife bore Alexander the Great and his sister Cleopatra of Macedon.

clue.text: Sets aside organ as belonging to evangelist

parts.note: the ear is an organ of hearing
Mark's, the possessive of Mark, author of the second Gospel

explanation.surface: A preacher reserves a body part as his own.
explanation.definitionFit: To reserve funds or items for a particular purpose is to earmark them.

clue.text: Demon precedes bad versifier for prolific Victorian novelist

indicators.note: precedes puts the demon word in front of what follows

parts.note: a troll is a malevolent creature of folklore

indicators.note: bad treats the poet's name as damaged, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe wrote verse as well as tales

explanation.surface: A fiend comes before a poor poet, to make way for a busy Victorian writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad versifier' looks like a poor poet, but 'bad' is the anagram signal working on the poet's name, and 'precedes' puts the demon first.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope wrote forty-seven novels, including the Barsetshire series, while working for the Post Office.

clue.text: Participant, like Hassall's piece

definitions.meaning: one taking part in a game or contest
Christopher Hassall wrote the verse drama The ... King

explanation.surface: Someone joins in, rather like a work by Hassall.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Hassall's play The Player King supplies the second sense; 'like' joins the two.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone who takes part in a sport is so called, and the word heads the title of Hassall's play.

clue.text: More offered in Latin, what Wells here sees as contemporary

definitions.text: More offered in Latin, what Wells here sees as contemporary

parts.words: More offered in Latin, what Wells here sees as contemporary
parts.note: Thomas More published his ideal commonwealth in Latin; H. G. Wells wrote an up-to-date version of it in 1905

explanation.walkthrough: 'More' is Sir Thomas More, not a comparative; his Utopia appeared in Latin in 1516, and Wells's A Modern Utopia updated it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wells's 1905 book imagined a present-day ideal state on the model of More's imaginary island.

clue.text: Gradually removed from Kipling's The Seven Seas (edited for dropped h's)

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

parts.words: Kipling's The Seven Seas (edited for dropped h's)

explanation.surface: A Kipling volume has been tidied so the Cockney dropped aitches disappear.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is se(AS ED)ited, across 'Seas (edited'. The talk of Kipling dialect and dropped aitches is scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease something out is to withdraw it slowly and carefully.

clue.text: Could be that a ropy chap defines them as non-canonical

definitions.note: an adjective standing for writings that are excluded from the canon, a plural noun

indicators.note: could be says the letters may become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A shabby fellow decides which scriptures are not in the official canon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' signals the anagram of A ROPY CHAP; 'defines them as' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Books outside the accepted biblical canon, such as Tobit, are grouped under this name.

clue.text: Logo which cannot help leaving an impression

definitions.text: Logo which cannot help leaving an impression

parts.words: Logo which cannot help leaving an impression
parts.note: a publisher's emblem stamped on a title page is literally made by pressing type onto paper

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving an impression' sounds like being memorable, but it means the inked imprint pressed on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: An emblem identifying a printer or publisher, like the Aldine dolphin and anchor, appears on its books.

clue.text: His tragedy came first

parts.note: Thomas ... co-wrote Gorboduc, usually counted the earliest English tragedy in blank verse

explanation.walkthrough: Gorboduc (1561), by Thomas Norton and Thomas Sackville, is reckoned the first English tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan poet and statesman co-authored Gorboduc, the pioneering English verse tragedy.

clue.text: Second highest American friend as dramatist

parts.note: top means highest
pard is American slang for partner or friend

explanation.surface: A second-in-line American pal becomes a playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Stoppard wrote Arcadia and Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead.

clue.text: Is he in Leinster? not entirely, this Friday writer

indicators.note: not entirely says only part of the following words is used, a run inside them

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man is in the Irish province of Leinster.
explanation.walkthrough: Leinster is an Irish province. 'Friday' is not a day here: Robert Heinlein wrote the novel Friday (1982).
explanation.definitionFit: The American science-fiction author published a 1982 novel titled Friday.

clue.text: Philip's daughter in Herodotus' Therma

definitions.meaning: Philip II of Macedon's daughter, half-sister of Alexander
the Macedonian town Herodotus called Therma was refounded under a new name

explanation.walkthrough: King Cassander named the city on the site of Therma after his wife, Philip II's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip II's daughter gave her name to the city refounded on ancient Therma, today's Thessaloniki.

clue.text: They provided Chopin's keys

parts.note: the Paris piano makers whose instruments the composer favoured and in whose salle he gave concerts

explanation.walkthrough: 'Keys' are piano keys: Chopin's preferred pianos came from the Paris firm founded by Ignaz Pleyel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Paris piano manufacturer founded by Ignaz Pleyel built the instruments Chopin chose to play.

clue.text: "They shall be commanded, on —— perpetual bondage, to depart." (Expulsion of the Moriscoes, Robert Southey)

definitions.text: "They shall be commanded, on —— perpetual bondage, to depart." (Expulsion of the Moriscoes, Robert Southey)

parts.words: "They shall be commanded, on —— perpetual bondage, to depart." (Expulsion of the Moriscoes, Robert Southey)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation: the missing words state the penalty threatened for refusing to leave Spain

explanation.walkthrough: A plain quotation to complete: the gap takes the phrase meaning 'under threat of'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'on pain of' means under penalty of, here the threat of slavery.

clue.text: Whitsuntide in the theatre

parts.note: the Christian feast of Whitsun shares its name with David Edgar's 1994 stage play

explanation.walkthrough: Whitsun is the feast's British name; David Edgar's 1994 play set in Eastern Europe carries the feast's other name.
explanation.definitionFit: The feast of the Holy Spirit's descent seven weeks after Easter is also the title of Edgar's play.

clue.text: One of Joyce's overseas residents?

parts.note: James Joyce wrote one play, whose title names people living away from their homeland

explanation.walkthrough: Joyce's only play is Exiles (1918); one person from that plural title is wanted, and Joyce himself lived abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone living banished or voluntarily away from their native land is so called, as in Joyce's play title.

clue.text: Mortimer's seasonal country house

parts.note: John Mortimer's novel Summer's Lease follows an English family renting a house in Tuscany for the summer

explanation.walkthrough: John Mortimer's Summer's Lease centres on an Italian holiday house let for the summer, hence 'seasonal'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rented Italian country residence, as in Mortimer's Tuscan novel, is called by this name.

clue.text: Roman School composer brothers from a north-eastern South American city

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, often called simply Rio

explanation.surface: Two composer brothers of the Roman School supposedly hail from a Brazilian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Felice and Giovanni Francesco Anerio were Roman composers of the late sixteenth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Felice and Giovanni Francesco Anerio, a pair of siblings, wrote sacred music in Palestrina's Roman tradition.

clue.text: Destroyer of pet bird in a no-return situation

indicators.note: in puts the parrot's name inside the other letters
return means the word no is read backwards

parts.note: Polly is the traditional name for a pet parrot

explanation.surface: Someone wrecks a pet parrot in a situation from which there is no going back.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'no-return' hides both the word and its signal; 'return' turns NO into ON, and 'in' sets the parrot inside.
explanation.definitionFit: In Revelation the angel of the bottomless pit bears a Greek name meaning the one who ruins.

clue.text: Hume's was in red

parts.note: Fergus Hume, author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, also wrote a novel about a performer in scarlet

explanation.walkthrough: Hume is not the philosopher but Fergus Hume, whose novel The Dancer in Red gives the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Fergus Hume's novel title names a stage performer of this kind dressed in scarlet.

clue.text: Swedish Nobel prize-winner applies for legal changes

indicators.note: changes says the letters of the words before it are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A Swedish laureate applies to have the law amended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changes' rearranges FOR LEGAL; 'applies' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Selma Lagerlof, author of Nils Holgersson, was the first woman to win the Nobel literature prize, in 1909.
